name: United Arab Emirates
summary: Muslims are bound by Sharia fixed shares and a one-third limit on bequests. Non-Muslims can now choose to have their own country's law apply, or leave a will under Federal Decree-Law 41 of 2022, and the DIFC and ADGM wills services let them register a will with full freedom. Trusts and private foundations exist inside the DIFC and ADGM free zones, not under onshore federal law.
reserved_share: Muslim estates: Sharia fixed shares apply and a bequest to a non-heir is limited to one third. For non-Muslims, Federal Decree-Law 41 of 2022 (Civil Personal Status, in force for deaths from 1 Feb 2023) lets a testator name beneficiaries (art. 11) within the Executive Regulations (Cabinet Decision 122 of 2023); without a will the spouse takes half and the rest goes to the children equally. Article numbers are from secondary commentary.
foreign_law_note: Reported by law-firm commentary: Decree-Law 41/2022 applies to non-Muslim citizens and residents, and the home country's law can be applied unless a registered will provides otherwise (art. 11(3)). A will registered with the DIFC Wills Service or the ADGM can cover assets and is enforced by those courts without Sharia shares. Applicants must be non-Muslim and at least 21. Abu Dhabi also has its own non-Muslim personal status law (Law 14 of 2021).
trust_note: Trusts and private foundations are available only in the free zones: the DIFC (DIFC Foundations Law, DIFC Law No. 3 of 2018, and a DIFC trust law) and the ADGM (Foundations Regulations 2017, English common-law trusts). Reported: the ADGM regime states that a transfer to a foundation cannot be set aside by reference to foreign forced heirship rules, and a foundation cannot bind a foreign court over land in that country. Onshore federal law has no general trust or private-foundation law. Mainland courts' treatment of a DIFC or ADGM trust over Sharia shares is not settled for Muslims.
open_questions: Primary text of Decree-Law 41 of 2022, its Executive Regulations and the article numbers were not retrieved; figures here come from law-firm commentary.
Statute number for the DIFC Wills Service is cited inconsistently (Dubai Law 15 of 2017 vs Dubai Law 2 of 2025); verify with DIFC Courts.
Whether a DIFC/ADGM will can bind onshore assets in each emirate (esp. real estate) needs confirming.

Hague Trusts Convention: The HCCH status table (checked 2026-10-16) lists 14 Contracting Parties; this country is not one of them and no UK, Dutch or Chinese extension covers it, so the 1985 Convention is not in force here.
